newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore election sparks U.S. meddling debate.
newsitem.headline: Singapore election sparks U.S. meddling debate.

text.p: Singapore's election campaign, which entered its fifth day on Saturday, has thrown up local "bread and butter" issues and also spurred debate on charges of U.S. meddling in the island republic's politics.
Singapore's opposition parties at election rallies have accused the government of not keeping down the costs of living, health care and ministerial wages.
But the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) has focused instead on the country's economic growth, stable politics and why it must stand up to what it calls foreign "interference" in domestic politics.
A United States State Department spokeswoman criticised Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other PAP candidates on Tuesday over their use of a housing upgrade programme to woo voters.
At issue was Goh's campaign statement that constituencies which elected the opposition would lose out on government housing renovations and development programmes.

In an editorial on Saturday, The Straits Times newspaper said: "Unfortunately, the subject of the remarks - Singapore - and their timing - the campaign for next week's general election - makes it impossible to believe they were purely declaratory."
"Instead, the remarks could not but have been meant to influence the course of political events here."
"That constitutes unwarranted interference in Singapore's domestic politics," the newspaper said.
Singapore's general election will be held on January 2, in which the PAP is assured a majority.

The PAP, which has won every election since 1959, was returned to power before a vote was cast in next Thursday's poll when opposition parties declared they would contest only 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
Ministers have called on Washington retract its criticism.
Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong also called on the opposition to make clear their stance on the U.S. comments.
The PAP declared on nomination day last Monday it would contest the election as a "local election", with voters being asked to back plans by PAP candidates to improve their wards.
Goh and other ministers have told voters they would lose out on housing renovation schemes that would increase the value of their homes if they elected an opposition candidate.

Goh said on Sunday he would respect the voters' choice if they elected someone from the opposition, but added: "Then you'll be left behind; then in 20, 30 years' time, the whole of Singapore will be bustling away and your estate, through your own choice, will be left behind. They become slums. That's my message."

The State Department spokeswoman said on Tuesday: "We believe that voters everywhere should be able to vote without fear of repercussions from government as a result of their responsibilities as citizens."
